analysis.one_liner: Imposes uniform federal rules on injury lawsuits, making losing parties pay attorney fees and limiting recoveries.
analysis.headline: Sen. McConnell's bill to rewrite injury-lawsuit rules nationwide, introduced with one Republican cosponsor, never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced the fifty states' individual tort laws with one federal set of rules for personal-injury and property-damage lawsuits. It would have required the losing side of a lawsuit to pay the winner's attorney fees, barred a defendant from being forced to pay more than its own share of fault, blocked most lawsuits by injured people who were intoxicated, and sharply limited civil-rights suits and money damages against local governments. Where state law conflicted, the federal rules would have overridden it.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses, product manufacturers, and liability insurers facing injury and product-liability suits would gain the most: the bill's stated purpose was 'greater certainty in the availability and cost of liability insurance' [S3]. Local governments would gain because the bill would bar money damages against them for most civil-rights violations, bar punitive damages, and shield 'good faith' actions [S3]. Defendants who prevail in any covered suit could collect their attorney fees from the losing plaintiff [S2].

how_it_helps.text: The bill's declared purpose is to provide 'greater certainty in the availability and cost of liability insurance' and to set 'reasonable limits on the potential exposure of individuals and businesses to liability' [S3].
It abolishes joint and several liability: a defendant could be made to pay only its own percentage share of fault, even if other responsible parties cannot pay or are not in the courtroom [S3].

It requires courts to award costs and attorney fees to the prevailing party in covered suits, with an exception only for losing parties poor enough to qualify for Legal Services Corporation help [S3].
It makes intoxication a complete defense when the injured person was more than 50 percent responsible for the accident, barring recovery entirely [S2].

It amends the civil-rights statute (42 U.S.C. 1983) to bar most lawsuits by organizations, block commercial and property-interest claims except discrimination cases, prohibit damages against a local government absent an official policy, and prohibit punitive damages [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People injured by defective products, malpractice, negligence, or civil-rights violations would bear the cost: they would face paying the defendant's legal bills if they lost, recover only the responsible defendant's fractional share of fault, lose cases outright if they were intoxicated, and have workers' compensation benefits deducted from awards [S3]. State legislatures would lose their authority to set their own liability rules, which the bill would preempt [S2].

drawbacks.text: Requiring the losing party to pay the winner's attorney fees would discourage people of ordinary means from filing valid claims, because a lost case against a well-funded corporation could mean owing the other side's legal bills; the bill's only carve-out is for people poor enough to qualify for Legal Services Corporation assistance [S3].
The bill would apply to every civil action filed after enactment, including suits where the injury or conduct occurred before the law passed [S3].

Ending joint and several liability means a catastrophically injured person whose harm was caused by several parties could collect only one defendant's fractional share if the others are insolvent, unknown, or shielded [S3].

The bill would strip civil-rights remedies: barring damages against local governments unless the violation flowed from an official policy, barring punitive damages, and excluding most organizational plaintiffs [S3].
The bill would override state tort law wholesale, including state rules crafted by state courts and legislatures over generations [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters argued that unpredictable litigation costs hurt American competitiveness and insurance affordability, and the bill would have made outcomes more predictable for businesses and insurers [S3]. But the way it achieved predictability was by shifting nearly every rule against the person bringing the suit: fee-shifting with only a narrow poverty exception, fractional recovery from multi-party harms, an intoxication bar, reduced awards for workers' compensation recipients, and narrowed civil-rights remedies [S2][S3]. The predictable benefits flow to defendants and insurers; the predictable costs fall on injured people, and on states whose own liability laws would be overridden [S2][S3].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee and later to its courts subcommittee, and it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-KY) introduced the Lawsuit Reform Act of 1991 in the Senate on November 15, 1991 [S1][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day [S5].
On January 22, 1992, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Courts and Administrative Practice, and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
The bill had a single cosponsor, a Republican senator [S4].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, with the bill still stuck in committee, never having reached the Senate floor [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured people kept the existing state-law rules for suing over defective products, negligence, malpractice, and civil-rights violations, including the ability to hold a fully insured defendant responsible for the full judgment. Businesses, insurers, and local governments lost the chance to have their lawsuit exposure capped by federal law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured people who kept their right to sue

for.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Lawsuit Reform Act of 1991 in the Senate.

for.name: 1 of 43 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it attracted no other Senate support.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Joseph Biden, D-DE)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral but never held a markup or advanced it; the record shows no committee action beyond the January 1992 referral to a subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and its only cosponsor were both Republicans, and no vote was ever taken, so the only visible support was Republican and the bill never faced a recorded partisan test.

industries.note: The bill's stated purpose was greater certainty in the availability and cost of liability insurance, achieved by capping what insurers would have to pay on injury and product-liability claims [S3]. The savings come out of compensation that injured people would otherwise receive.

industries.industry: Product manufacturers and businesses facing tort suits
industries.note: The bill would end joint and several liability, shift attorney fees to losing plaintiffs, bar intoxicated claimants, and reduce awards by workers' compensation benefits [S2][S3]. Each rule lowers the cost and risk of being sued, at the price of weaker remedies for people harmed by their products or conduct.

The bill would amend the civil-rights statute to bar money damages against local governments absent an official policy, bar punitive damages, and shield actions taken in good faith [S3]. People whose constitutional rights are violated by local governments would have fewer avenues to recover.

Fee-shifting to the prevailing party, capped by reference to the losing party's own fee arrangement, would make taking injury cases on contingency riskier and shrink the market for plaintiff-side legal work [S3]. This industry's fortunes rise and fall with ordinary people's access to the courts.
